tests.description: Commands we decline to run even with approval, matched by command word and by the last part of a path. Only the destructive spellings of git subcommands are refused, and only in the first argument position.

Each recognized command contributes its own effects. An unrecognized command, an unknown flag, a non-literal command word and a leading assignment are all unrecognized. In a sequence, echo contributes nothing whatever its arguments, because bash runs it.
A redirect writes a file whatever the verb is, so it contributes std::write independently. A variable target or any other redirect kind is unrecognized.

The whole string gets one plan: refused if any command anywhere is refused, one std::bash if any command is unrecognized, otherwise the union of narrow effects. Chains are walked, so `true && rm -rf /tmp/x` is refused rather than approvable.
A narrow plan runs the tree it classified (whitespace normalized); a broad plan runs the caller's text verbatim.
A single fully-literal echo computes its own output and never touches a shell. An expansion, a flag, or a sequence sends it to bash.

A single literal redirected echo computes its content and writes it, with no shell. The `>` and `>>` rows differ only in mode, which is the difference between overwriting and appending. A variable TARGET is unrecognized entirely; a variable in the ARGUMENTS is still recognized and goes to bash raising std::write with no content — approval of the destination, not the bytes. Non-write plans report only the fields their Execution variant carries.
Payload values, not just effect names. A staged diff and an unstaged diff raise the same effect name, so only the payload distinguishes them.
The std::write interrupt carries the bytes, so a policy that inspects what is being written still can.
A literal echo returns its text with no interrupt and no shell.
The narrow question REPLACES the broad one. Approving std::git::status runs the command; a second std::bash prompt would fail the run on an unmatched interrupt.
A refused command fails without raising anything, so there is nothing to approve.
A sequence runs in one bash call, so its output is bash's — including the newline behavior v2 got wrong.

A broad plan records why: the parser message, the first unrecognized command, the audit rule, or an unrenderable tree. A narrow or refused plan has no reason.

tests.description: A grep path that does not exist makes the command unrecognized; planFor does not throw.
On the bash path the payload carries the pattern as written, the file, the booleans from the letters, no cap, and no regex flags.

A lone grep whose flags and pattern translate exactly runs through the grep tool's search, with no shell. A flag the tool lacks, a pattern that does not translate, a directory without -r, a pipe, or -w with a non-word edge sends it to the bash path. A flag after the file is fine here, where no real grep reads the arguments.

The shell-free payload carries the regex the search uses (escaped for -F), the u flag so . matches a whole character, and the 1000-match cap; a file search splits into the real parent directory and the file name.

Each row runs the shell-free path and the real grep program on the same command and compares the lines. The fixtures hold no skipped or ignored files, so a difference is a translation or rendering bug. Each row first checks that its command really runs shell-free.
A lone grep asks one std::grep question and no shell question, prints the lines the way grep does, and says which folders the search skipped.

tests.description: A lone grep of a folder where .gitignore ignores only some entries (dot files, compiled .js files) still runs the tool's search, because the search finds the rest.
Every flattened command says whether it reads a pipe: the first stage of a pipe does not, every command in a later stage does, and a command outside the pipe does not.

A grep with no path in a later stage of a pipe searches the previous stage's output and reads no file, so it contributes nothing beyond its redirects. -r still wins (it reads the working directory), a named path wins over the pipe, a grep outside the pipe still reads stdin, the flag table still applies, and a line of recognized commands with no effect asks std::bash by the audit rule.
